explanation: Young sunflowers do track the Sun as they grow, but once the flowers open, most heads stay facing east. Warming up in the morning sun helps them draw more bees.

claims.text: Mature sunflower heads do not follow the Sun across the sky each day; most stay facing east.
Young, growing sunflower plants turn to follow the Sun during the day.
East-facing sunflower heads warm up faster in the morning and attract more pollinating insects than west-facing heads.

writerNotes: Self-check (guide 9.3), all eleven codes confirmed true. The selfCheck field itself is left out because the CNT-1 item schema refuses it as an unknown key, so the codes are recorded here. lint: content:check reports no errors and no warnings for this item. claims: three listed. c1 is high because it is the key of a counterintuitive item, so C26 sets it high; the tooling's riskReason enum has no counterintuitive value yet (guide v1.1 adds one), so checker_doubt stands in for it. I raised c3 to high (checker_doubt) because it rests on one well-known study rather than general knowledge; one search on sunflower heliotropism should cover c1 and c3. c2 is standard. datasets: no pinned dataset in content/datasets/manifest.json covers animal or plant biology, so none applies and every high-risk claim needs web evidence from checker A. rivalTest: argued for true: the plant's name in several languages means 'turns with the sun', and young plants really do; the statement says 'in full bloom', which is the stage that stops turning. That wording is what makes it a myth and not a trick. volatility: evergreen, a settled fact that cannot change; no time words, and nothing rests on knowledge newer than mid-2026. regional: sunflowers are grown worldwide. style: Oxford spelling, plain hyphens only, explanation of 30 words. myths: screened against content/reference/myths.json; no entry matches; the belief is common but not yet on the list. mystery and encore: nothing of either kind in a true/false item. doubts: none on the key.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: Mature plants' permanent eastward orientation makes for warmer flower faces, which may be responsible for a large increase in pollinator visits, according to a Science news summary, which reports the figure as five times more than in west-facing mature plants. Disputed: A 2024 study by Takács and colleagues, cited in later work, found that the pollinator visits of sunflower inflorescences in Helianthus annuus plantations are independent of head orientation.

claimResults.note: The 2016 study linked warmer east-facing heads to about five times more pollinator visits, but a 2024 field study found visits independent of head orientation. Sources disagree, so the claim fails as written (§9.5.2).

issues.note: The explanation's second sentence ('Warming up in the morning sun helps them draw more bees') rests on the 2016 study and is disputed by a 2024 field study (Takács and colleagues). Rewrite it to what the sources agree on, for example that east-facing heads warm up faster in the morning sun, or drop the pollinator clause. The key is unaffected.

evidence.restatement: Mature sunflower heads stop following the Sun and most face east.

A revise: c3 says east-facing heads warm faster and attract more pollinators, which rests on the 2016 Science study and is contradicted by a 2024 field study that found visits independent of head orientation. Peer-reviewed sources conflict, so c3 fails as written and a tiebreak cannot confirm it; dropping the clause changes a claim, which needs two fresh checks.
